home.bio1: I'm a fullstack developer and researcher based in Bordeaux. I fell into computer science young and never left, drawn by the idea that code isn't just tooling, it's infrastructure for society. That curiosity led me to distributed systems, cryptography, and eventually to the question I keep coming back to: how do we establish trust without a central authority?
home.bio2: The more I look at the web's architecture, the clearer the problem becomes. Every system of trust we've built still relies on someone at the center vouching for everyone else: certificate authorities, social login, identity providers. It works, until it doesn't. I'm interested in what comes after.
home.bio3: Today I build production SSI infrastructure at Verana and 2060.io, DIDComm messaging, verifiable credentials, trust registries. I also created Credat, an open-source library that brings the same trust model to AI agents, giving autonomous systems verifiable identities and scoped delegation. As agents become more capable and autonomous, the question of how services verify them, and who authorized them to act, becomes urgent.
home.bio4: I'm 20. I've bet everything on decentralized identity being one of the foundational problems of the next era, for people and for the agents acting on their behalf.
home.bio5: Before tech, I spent seven years training as a high-level parkour athlete, competing and teaching across France. In 2025, I co-founded PKBA, now the largest parkour club in Nouvelle-Aquitaine. Discipline, pattern recognition, and learning from failure fast, sports and systems thinking have more in common than they appear.

research.title: Research
research.intro: My research interests lie at the intersection of distributed systems, applied cryptography, and digital identity. I'm particularly interested in systems that give individuals control over their personal data while maintaining interoperability across organizations and borders.

areas.title: Decentralized Identity & DIDs
areas.body: Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) provide a foundation for self-sovereign identity by allowing entities to create and control their own identifiers without permission from any central authority. I study the design trade-offs between different DID methods (did:web, did:peer, did:key) and their implications for security, privacy, and scalability.

areas.title: Privacy-Preserving Credential Systems
areas.body: Verifiable Credentials enable portable, tamper-evident digital attestations. I'm interested in selective disclosure mechanisms (BBS+ signatures, SD-JWT) that allow holders to share only the minimum necessary information, and in zero-knowledge proof techniques that enable predicate proofs without revealing underlying data.

areas.title: Trust Frameworks & Governance
areas.body: Decentralized systems still need trust anchors. I work on trust registry architectures that allow ecosystems to define and enforce governance rules, who can issue what, which credentials are accepted where, and how trust decisions are made at scale.

areas.title: DIDComm & Secure Messaging
areas.body: DIDComm is a messaging protocol that enables secure, private communication between identity agents. I work on production implementations of DIDComm v2, including message routing, encryption, and protocol negotiation for credential exchange workflows.

questions: How can trust registries be made both decentralized and practically governable?
What are the formal privacy guarantees of different selective disclosure schemes under realistic adversarial models?
How can SSI systems achieve meaningful interoperability across jurisdictions with different legal frameworks?
What are effective revocation mechanisms that preserve holder privacy?
